title: Kyle Pitts Sr. speaks to the media on Atlanta Falcons contract extension | Press Conference
text: Hey Kyle, how are you man? Congratulations. >> Hey, how you doing brother? Thank you. >> Yes sir. Uh how did all this happen? Like when did you know it was about to happen and just how excited are are you to remain in Atlanta long term? >> Yeah, first I I didn't know it was going to happen. I was just once I signed the franchise tag, it was more so okay, that was that was my uh option. I mean, not my options, sorry, my um opportunity that, you know, Atlanta picked it back up to give me another year to showcase and then it was just time to squeeze the rag and just grind. Um it was fortunate that I got the call and and the interest in the long term and when it happened, it was it was pretty great. >> How much does it help you when this is a a whole new regime for them to come in and invest in you early on? Is this kind of a sign in your eyes that they really um are are are happy with how how you've impressed them and and just kind of how do you view it on that end of hey it's a brand new regime? I think it's uh great. But the first thing for me is just my expression of gratitude for this uh organization with Matt um with Ian and with course the fansky and the whole front office to be able to do that. And uh it's just it's a it's always good to know when people people like you and for for them to invest and trust that um I I have a lot more to go. It's is pretty cool to to see and and feel. All right, we'll go to Josh and then Joe. >> Josh, I think you might be muted. >> Okay, there's so many buttons. >> You mentioned Matt in your in your answer. uh you know when he came back here um you know what what do you do you think that helped your cause a guy that you have played with and what do you remember about playing with him your rookie year? >> Um I think it helps tremendously um with a with a guy like Matt in the building around and just him being in the in the meetings and uh just on the field in practice. It's it's been great knowing him and he's the exact same just in a office now. um he's still getting on me about the small details. He's giving different, you know, small tidbits on how I can be a better leader and professional um as he did my rookie year. So, it's great having him back and I I appreciate it. >> What What now do you do you feel like this ups the pressure on you? Do you take it, you know, do you feel like, okay, now more is expected of me or did you always feel that way? >> No, it's I never really put pressure on myself. is more so just knowing what I can do and what I bring to the table. Um just all I want to do is be an asset to this offense and I've you know thank God in this in this organization for now extending me is the pressure doesn't that's not something that's even in my mind is more so just now to whom you know much is given much is required and now I have to give what I what I require. >> Thank you Kyle. >> Yep. Kyle, congratulations. Um, just wanted to ask you just about kind of the the continuity that's really been built now with part of this is with your signing on that offensive side of the football with Drake, with Bjon, with Chris Lindstöm, Jake Matthews. How can that continuity help this team going forward, especially under this new regime? >> I think it's great. Um, all the guys you just named, we're super close and we're we're kind of the guys that are uh have been here, you know, for a good amount of time the these past four to five years. Um, and myself, I would say I'm the most quiet of all the names you said, but I like to listen and watch Chris work, watch Drake work, watch um Jake work. Um, all of those guys are very professional and it's it's great to be alongside them and see how we can, you know, bring other people alongside us with us so that this offense is rolling. >> Do you feel like now that you've signed this deal and you're, you know, you're going to be around a little bit longer term that you are stepping into more of that that leadership role with some of these other young younger players on the team and on this offense? >> I mean, it's something I've been doing for a couple years now. just trying I wouldn't say I'm more so like the rah guy. So maybe that kind of give the persona of you know he he's not a super loud leader but I may pull you aside or show you by example bring you with me. Um that's that's kind of what I've been doing and I won't change who I am. Um if anything I'll just like I said the guys that I'm bringing alongside with me you know hope they do the same for somebody else. >> All right Maria. >> Oh congratulations. >> Thank you. How you doing Maria? >> I'm good. How are you? >> Good. >> So, what has Kevin Koger's relationship meant with you just in terms of your development as a player and that coach player relationship? >> Me and Coach Koger is is a has like a the brother I never wanted. Um, when it's time to to grind and compete, he he he coaches me hard and he's helping me learn the game mentally to to be a mentally faster and and stronger player. And when I mean that, I mean just being able to, you know, read the defense on and off the field things in terms of life. Uh he he's been he's been around the the block a couple times. So just to for him to be someone I can be free with and and when it's time to get, you know, serious and you know, when we practicing and in meetings, we lock in and it's just it's great to have him as a coach. >> How would you describe your evolution as a tight end since your time here in Atlanta? I would say to start just obviously as a rookie you start out raw. Um, and I learned behind some core guys and in Hayden Hurst and and Lee uh Lee Smith and then I had guys like Janu and Michael Puit my cole. I mean all those guys are played 10 years at minimum and it's it was cool to each year go from trying to stay above water as a rookie to each year it getting better um learning the playbook faster and and learning how to play faster. So, you know, from day one to now, I feel like it's night and day. >> Appreciate you. Thank you. >> Thank you. >> All right, we'll go to Allison next. >> Hey, Kyle. Congrats. >> Hey, how you doing, Alison? >> Good. So, when we were talking with Drake after he signed his contract, he said, you know, he believed in this team and the ability to win a Super Bowl and he wanted to be legendary with this team and help win the first one. So, what do you want to do and help accomplish with this team? I want to do my part very well in whatever the coach asks me to do. Um whether that is blocking, run, running, being a being a leader to the rookies or, you know, pulling somebody aside to come along with me to do anything. Whatever needs to be done for us to get to meaning football, I'm I'm I'm in. And that's how how I have been. And now it's just more enhanced. I feel like like Drake said like we have the team, we have the guys. I' I've been here. I've seen it. I've seen four years of five years of ball. I'm not saying I mean there's a lot more to come, but knowing what we have here is something special and it's just, you know, us to take to this next level. >> Yeah. And it feels like when you're healthy, it's like you've gone up every year, whether it's yards or or touchdowns. Do you feel like maybe that like some of your best ball is still yet to come for you? >> 100%. I I think it's a lot more out there. Um, a lot more to get and a lot of more things to keep grinding towards. >> All right, we'll go to Jarvis Davis. >> Hey Kyle, congratulations on your contract, man. >> What's going on, Jarvis? Thank you. >> Good, man. Um, I just want to kind of go back to when you right around when the spring when you were talking about being back and you referenced um, your son being like one of the part of the cubes. I just want to kind of It seems like you were like so comfortable like being in in the place that you're in right now. Is that a good assessment as far as like you've going you talking about your rookie year and being raw and just kind of taking all things in. Do you feel like you're in a better place now just as far as firmly set on the foundation now that you got your contract and just being in the league for for so long? >> Definitely not comfortable. I would just say it's another opportunity, another opportunity to be uh influential on this on and off the field here and in this city Atlanta. Um definitely not com I mean like I said comfortable or you know complacent at all. Um and the cubes are Matt Ryan's children. That's I was I was cool with them. Yeah. >> Okay. I got you. I got you. And you know, it's just it's cool to see and you know, I'm here for hopefully the rest of my career and I just want to keep keep doing well each year and you know, us get to that over that hump. >> And how's your relationship with Matt now that he's, you know, in that the position he's in as a president of football? >> I would say it's it's kind of the same. Matt's not he didn't change. Uh now he just has an office. And that's kind of like what I try and tell people. I mean, he's the same person. He still curse you out. he still pull you to the side and and then coach you hard. It's just from a different uh standpoint and he's he's still the ultimate competitor. So, you know, it's it's cool to have him around. >> Thank you, man. >> All right, we'll go back to Daniel. Yeah, Kyle, kind of wonder um because last month when we had you, you mentioned the the chats you had with God and then when we had Koger last month, you mentioned a chat that he had with you, I think after the New Orleans game, the maybe mid November one about just a chat then that kind of helped you a lot. I I wonder from a a mental viewpoint, is this is as fresh as mature as you feel or have felt? I guess. >> Um I would say each year is it gets better each day? Um, I'm constantly always, you know, selft talk and and confidence is a big thing in in in life, not even just football, but just to be able to, you know, when I had when I was going through that funk, I feel like to be able to get back on track and get back in my book, that was that was the main thing for me and and knowing what helps me go. >> When do you think you reached a point where you could kind of look in a mirror and say, "Okay, I need to improve here. I need to improve here." And then along those lines, when do you think you reached a point with God where you could also say, "Hey, I really need this. I need help here. >> I would say that's every day looking in the mirror, finding something you can get better at. And then with my faith, that's like I that's the same thing. Every day trying to draw closer to him. Um God is the the driver of this of this car and I'm just, you know, trying to find ways to be better for him and myself. >> All right, back to Joe. Oh, Joe, I think you're on mute. >> There it is. I pulled a Josh. That's what we call it. >> Oh, okay. >> All right, Josh. You gota live with that now. >> Ma, >> you hear that, Josh? Yeah. Um, now that now that we're through OTAAS, Kyle, I'm just curious if you are if you feel like an identity to this offense is is starting to emerge. I know obviously a lot of that's going to come in training camp as well, but just uh if you feel excited, especially for you, and how your production could uh benefit from from this offense. Uh yeah, definitely definitely. I think we're we're growing one and coach Stfansky says that he he had a quote that kind of stuck with me is is if you don't define your identity, somebody else will. And that's something that we're trying to implement in our offense and in this team and and growing one, but as offense specifically, I think we're we're growing one and and going into camp. That'll be uh a continuation of OTAAS. >> And if I could do a followup that is in no way related to that, but I asked Drake the same thing. you know, when you get to this point in your career, you know, you've got kind of an era of your, you know, career wrapped up. Is there any moment that stands out for you as a personal highlight, whether it's something that you did in a game or a team moment or something off the field? If there's just anything that stands out from your Falcons career so far, >> getting drafted, that's that's what I I I'll go with. Being able to get the chance to come to this next level and play at the highest level is a been a dream of mine since I was started playing the game. So, that's that's probably my most favorite thing. All right, go ahead, Alison. >> Kind of going off of that a little bit, when you mentioned that you hopefully wanted to play the rest of your career here with Atlanta, I guess. What would that mean to you, especially for a team that took a chance on you with the fourth overall pick and still sees a lot in you? I think I think that's something of like I like consistency and I like just want to stick it through because there was times in you know when I committed to University of Florida they were 4 and seven the year before and then those next three years we went to a new year six and then got to the playoffs my last year. So it's just a a testament to myself and just staying patient. That's just what I'm what I like to do. I feel like we have the team and this is the organization that is going to break through and it it may not be on everyone else's timeline or you know on on their uh what I'll say date of when you know it should be done but it's just stay staying down staying patient.

title: The Bengals' Next Extension? DJ Turner's Agent Shares Cryptic Post
text: The countdown to training camp continues. Players are spending some time off before returning to Payor Stadium where the front office appears to be putting in more offseason work. Are the Bengals actually about to agree to an extension with DJ Turner? Let's break down what Turner's agent shared and more right here on Cincinnati Bengals Talk. I'm Andrew Fox Miller. Thank you for joining us on this Monday. Whether you're watching or listening, James Rapin of Bengals.com is currently airing live on his daily morning show, First Word. And I'm sure one of the bigger topics he's covering this morning involves quarterback DJ Turner. Look, the Bengals have delivered an exciting off season so far. Arguably the most exciting offseason in franchise history, certainly in the Joe Burrow era. I don't need to list every bullet point as to why this offseason has been so noteworthy. And maybe there are a few of you out there that actually consider it to be underwhelming for reasons I wouldn't understand. But at the very least, I think there's one word for this off seasonason that any fan of the Cincinnati Bengals would agree with. That word would be unexpected. You can pick your moment or your top moments. When you realize the Bengals were delivering the unexpected. Maybe it was when they signed Brian Cook, who was considered by many to be the top free agent safety out there in 2026. Maybe the unexpected hit you when they signed Boy Maf or Jonathan Allen. I would certainly hope it would eventually hit you when they traded their 10th overall pick for Dexter Lawrence. Maybe you experienced the unexpected at the very beginning of it all when they resigned Daltton Riser. Remember that? Remember that? I mean, like it feels like a lifetime ago. The familiar became unfamiliar. And for some of you, the unfamiliar just kept stacking. Restructuring Joe Burrow's contract would have felt like a major headline in past offseasons. And while still noteworthy, it wasn't even close to the biggest headline of the past several months. There's still work to be done. Of course, that's always the case in the NFL. And one of the bigger lingering questions on this team is what players, if any, they lock into contract extensions while they still can. More specifically, what will this team end up doing about DJ Turner? Among the players entering their final year of their rookie deals, including Dax, Miles Murphy, and Chase Brown, DJ Turner is at the top of the to-do list. Whether that's signing him to an extension or deciding to pass on Turner for whatever reason, and put your resources into the other players I just mentioned, the dominoes begin to fall once that decision is made. And DJ Turner's agent appears to be suggesting that a decision is possibly happening sooner than many of us, including myself, might have expected. Turner's agent, Andre ODM, posted a cryptic Instagram story on Sunday where he includes Turner's Instagram handle with the caption CB1 quarterback 1 calculated. Before I break this down a bit, and look, it's a Tom and Jerry meme. It's not like I'm doing a deep dive like I'm Mike Santaga watching all 22 film or something. But does this mean Turner and the Bengals have actually reached a deal? Of course not. Doesn't necessarily mean that. They could simply be in the middle of negotiations and maybe there's some optimism. Maybe Turner's agent is simply saying that they're calculating the bag that Turner is due. But the reason I think there's more to this than simply posting a meme while spinning wheels in negotiations is because of the sign that reads soon in the background. Soon DJ Turner will get a stack of cash. Okay. Well, if it's soon, then I have to think it's while Turner is still in stripes, not in 2027. And if it's soon and calculated, past tense, by the way, in that caption if you haven't noticed, calculated, and we're in the month of June, do we think Turner's agent is expecting a wait time that extends into the regular season? I wouldn't think so. But we know things fall apart, discussions change, they can linger, stall, things happen. Nonetheless, it's noteworthy. We'll talk about that a bit more after a word from our local local sponsors. First of which is Christian Husky of Cypsey Klein Realtors. Christian is a Bengals fan and a Cincinnati Bengals talk supporter. He stuck with us as a local sponsor all season long and even through this off season. I highly doubt Christian expected the Bengals to have the offseason we've witnessed. Imagine the Bengals having the an offseason like they did in 2025. Imagine telling a YouTube channel, "Yeah, I'm going to stay on board as a sponsor throughout another one of those off seasons." He took that risk and remained loyal to us and and that's a trait I look for in anyone representing me or my interests. That's what you should want in a realtor. Buying a home is a big deal. Whether it's your first time or fourth, give Christian the opportunity to help you in that process. Visit him online at sipsccline.com/husky. That's caschristian husky. And now a word from our newest local sponsor, Joe Morgan Honda. Stop into Joe Morgan Honda in Monroe today and check out the great lease and finance specials going on now on all new CRVS, Civics, Accords, Pilots, and Ridgelines. All priced and ready to go. Honda quality and Morgan Integrity. Proud to be part of the Voss Auto Network. Joe Morgan Honda. Stop by in person on State Route 63 off I75 in Monroe or online at joeorgganhonda.com. I may have to go visit Joe Morgan Honda and test drive something. Maybe make a video out of it. Maybe I'll do an entire video where the latest Bengals topics I'm talking about that while test driving a car. I'll see if James is on board. I'm sure he'll find a way to make it competitive though, like a street race or like street race where he's the one on foot. Something like that. Anyway, DJ Turner, if you asked me in January of this year whether or not DJ Turner will remain with the Bengals after this season, it would get a yes from me. No hesitation. I still think that, but I've also sensed since then with all of the big moves the team has made, there's some concern swirling out there. And look, I'm not going to break down his market value or cap hit or any of that, but the the concern is, can they afford to pay DJ Turner? If he's roughly 20 million a year, more or less, is that realistic? The answer will always be yes, by the way, until I see evidence of otherwise. Other teams have figured it out. The Bengals can figure it out. Maybe it has been figured out already. I don't know. But regardless, and and I was leading up to this earlier, discussions are discussions. Until there's a signed contract, a cryptic post from a player's agent isn't confirming anything, of course. But it's still noteworthy. It's noteworthy the Bengals could be reaching a deal with a player who was one of the very few bright spots on a defense that was awful in 2025. a player who had a breakout season, a player who would have been a pro bowler had that defense not been so historically bad. He's going to cost money. Of course, he should. And the Bengals should do whatever they can to pay him what he's worth. Even if you keep Dax Hill, the quarterback room is thin after that. They didn't draft DJ Turner's replacement this year. I don't think they plan on drafting his replacement in 2027. They shouldn't expect to find that replacement, even if that were the plan. Turner was tied for second among all cornerbacks in passes defended in 2025. At 25 years old, he's the future of your secondary. And even though he addresses contract status with reporters where he seems to have zero interest in holding out or being any sort of distraction during training camp, >> how important is it for everyone to be here, whether or not you have a new contract or not, just to be here and bought in right now? >> Yeah, I mean, it's big. Um, it's big for sure. There's there's no blueprint in it in into everything though. So, I mean, it definitely was a big part to coming in. You know, we had a lot of new faces on defense. You know, get around everybody and, you know, just being being around the team. He's fine. It's fine. I'm going to just leave the contract talk to in-house and my agent. Um, I'm just here to work with. And honestly, that's what I've been that's what I'm focused on right now. >> The Bengals should still be racing the clock to extend him as though it will be a distraction. Turner might not act in a way that is a distraction, but the very fact that your two starting quarterbacks aren't secured beyond 2026 can contribute to distractions. The Bengals have executed deals in ways I've never experienced this off season. The work may not be easy, but some decisions should be easy ones. This is a four-down unit. Wants to play cover three from a two-high shell. Wants to mix in quarters and then play a lot of cover one. So, that aligns with really that family of defense, even though they're not part of it. So, it's like the adjacent part of that. I mean, even some of the things that Hafley was doing with the Packers, you start seeing show up a little bit of it. So, philosophically, this isn't a Ravens 2.0 system. So, we're not looking like the Seahawks. This isn't a Fangio-adjacent system that you see that mainly wants to play from a two-high shell. This is really kind of its own thing, but who they've aligned with has really been that Saleh kind of base defense that you see coming really out of San Francisco. >> Yeah, which is interesting for a variety of reasons. You hit on one of them there. And that again, this is not a branch off of that tree. It's more of mirroring what they've seen. And that's also what they've seen is what a lot of people see around the league is a response to the proliferation of the Shanahan kind of McVay system and the base coverages that are best equipped to counter that, which is not the Seattle three, where Saleh comes from. And then evolves into more of these quarters things where you're matching certain routes. And now, of course, as the constant cycle of football continues, um there's a punch back. Here we go into like course 300 about the next evolution, what's happening next. Like, it's not quite the backbone, but I think what it does is it uh unlocks a lot. So, can you can you elaborate on that for us about the role the safeties have in this particular system the Patriots are building out? >> Yeah, and I think Woodson really is your traditional down safety. He's a big dude, he plays really well near the box. The problem that you ran in last year was that they were trying to run a hybrid scheme, which look, in a perfect world, ask any coach, you would love in the modern day to have a left and a right safety that can do everything. And really when you seen some of these two-high structures, now remember, cover uh you know, two-high doesn't mean cover two or quarters, it just means we're going to play from depth. When you see that, you really need safeties to be able to adjust. I think where we've gotten now in this landscape is really we need to have a nickel. However that guy is, where you have kind of a Marcus Jones is really on the smaller side, he's more of a coverage nickel. Well, part of the problem you had last year was that your two edges were not very big. So, you had Clowney and you had uh Harold Landry. Both of those guys are not going to set the edge. Right? So, you had to get into one of the ways that they were they were really trying to manufacture kind of pressure and then kind of a better run structure was by dropping either Woodson or Hawkins into that kind of apex down near the boundary. And so, what I think you see this year in this system is we need to play from a two-high shell on early downs. But we need to have really an enforcer near the box, which I think Woodson is going to be. If you look at Kevin Byard, not great near the box. They You know, Dennis Allen put him near the box to just kind of be like, "Hey, you know, well, he might be down there just so you don't know what we're doing cuz like Brisker was the enforcer for them last year." >> Right. >> Byard's not great in the new box. One of the best post safeties uh or deep safeties really in the NFL really past couple years. I think you're going to see a little bit more of that cover one mentality, which is what they really wanted to play. I mean, that's why you go and get a guy >> like Christian Gonzalez and then a guy like uh you know >> Carlton Davis, yeah. >> Carlton Davis. Had a brain fart. title: Details on Chris Johnson's ALS diagnosis | NFL Live
text: We're back on NFL Live and we got the news this morning that former Titans, Jets, and Cardinals running back Chris Johnson announced that he was diagnosed last year with ALS, a disease that attacks nerve cells that control muscles throughout the body and for which there is no known cure. He told his story to Michael Strahan on ABC's Good Morning America earlier today. >> You chosen to share some personal news today and it takes a tremendous amount of courage to share it. What would you like for people to know? >> First, I want people to know that I'm still me. ALS has changed what my body can do, but it hasn't changed who I am. >> In 2025 at the age of 39, Johnson was diagnosed with ALS. The disease progressing so rapidly that he now uses his eyes to trigger speech generating device to speak. >> Why do you want to share this now? >> Because if sharing my story helps even one person get diagnosed sooner, inspires more research, or gives another family hope, then it's worth it. >> Johnson says he was in the prime of his life, working out daily, and running errands with his four children until ALS changed everything. >> Let's go back to last year. When did you notice that something was off? >> I first noticed weakness in my right hand. At first, it was little things like my grip didn't feel right and I wasn't as strong as I've always been. >> His wife, Britney, thought it was something much simpler. >> Britney, what did you think it was at the time? >> I thought because um of football and you know, his career, that it had to be something with that, maybe a pinched nerve or something along those lines, but never ALS. >> And what did doctors tell you initially about your condition? >> We hoped it was something else, but after thorough testing, they finally came down with a diagnosis of ALS. They told us about a medication that might extend life by a few months. Then they told us to get our affairs in order. It was hard hearing that, but after watching Good Morning America and seeing Dr. Merit with Eric Dane, we reached out to her. She was willing to think more creatively, offering experimental treatments that might help and advance research. >> Dr. Merit Sickovich is a neurologist and leading ALS researcher at Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. >> Chris has been on standard of care, which is about three different medications that slow down the illness, but he was also part of a a clinical trial of therapy that decreases inflammation, and I think that helped him a lot. >> With no family history of ALS, doctors believe his is a case of sporadic ALS, the most common form of the disease, affecting about 90% of patients, occurring randomly in people with no known family history of ALS. >> That's one of the reasons this disease can be so shocking. It can happen to someone who never expected it. >> And for me, it's shocking. It's hard to process it for me because I know you, Chris, from just an incredible athlete that you are. How do you process it? >> Honestly, I don't know if you ever fully process it. At first, you're in shock, then you realize you have two choices. You can give up or you can fight. I chose to fight. >> And and Brittany, what was it like for you when you found out that Chris had ALS? >> All I could think about was our kids and how young they are. Just you're in denial. You want it to be anything else. You want the doctors to be wrong. The life that we previously had is like now a thing of the past, but we're still hopeful. We're hopeful, you know, that a breakthrough will happen and that or, you know, God a miracle will happen, you know. >> And what kind of support has helped you the most through this? >> Without a doubt my wife Brittany. She hasn't left my side through any of this. My kids are also a huge part of why I keep going. Every day I wake up wanting more time with them to make more memories and just be their dad. They give me a reason to keep fighting. >> Brittany the unsung hero of all caregivers. So what has this been like for you? >> Oh it's tough. It's tough like we have good days, we have bad days, you know, and our life has shifted so much and it's a heavy workload but I have no doubt that this is what you know, I was called to do. >> So how has it progressed since you've been diagnosed? >> It's continued to progress much faster than I ever imagined. I want people to understand just how quickly ALS can attack your body. Just over a year ago I was picking up my 7 year old daughter so she make a wish with her birthday cake. Today I couldn't do that. >> And what do you hope people or you wish people understood about living with ALS? >> That your mind stays sharp. People sometimes look at the physical disability and assume you're not still the same person inside. I still think the same, I still dream, I still love my family. My body just doesn't cooperate. >> What are the doctors telling you about the treatment and the progression? >> Having doctors who are willing to collaborate and explore every reasonable option has meant a lot to my family and me. Right now there isn't a cure but we're seeing more research, more clinical trials and more promising ideas than ever before. Seeing how hard these doctors and researchers are working gives me hope. As long as they're fighting for people with ALS, I'm going to keep fighting, too. >> Titans controlling owner Amy Adams Strunk released a statement on behalf of the organization that read in part, "Learning this news is extremely difficult and we will support Chris every step of the way throughout his journey. We're holding him and his family close and join our fans around the world in expressing our love for Chris." The sports world rallying around Chris Johnson after the news of his ALS diagnosis. Messages of support coming from everywhere, including his former college team, East Carolina University, expressed love and support for their former star tweeting, "We love you." Patrick Mahomes sending his prayers writing, "Man, praying for CJ2K." And former Patriots wide receiver Julian Edelman reflecting on Johnson's career calling him one of his favorite guys to watch and compete against and an ultimate competitor. This story just another reminder of how cruel life can be sometimes. You just never know when your whole life can change, but it doesn't mean we can't reflect on the great times. And Chris Johnson's magic on the football field deserves to be celebrated, too. His 2,509 scrimmage yards in the 2009 season is a record that stands today still. As we head to break, let's look back at the 2009 season that saw Johnson run for over 2,000 yards. >> I kept putting [music] up big numbers and big numbers and it went from it being a joke to this guy [music] really got a chance of going for 2,000 yards. >> Chris Johnson has done it. He has gone over 2,000 yards becoming the sixth [music] player in NFL history to do it. >> Oh.
